extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical geometry / readers of Euclid (Heath edition)
extracted.subtask_description: Expositions and constructions from Euclid Books IV–V: methods for inscribing/circumscribing regular polygons (pentagon, hexagon, 15-gon) and the formal definitions and conceptual criteria for ratio and proportion (Eudoxean theory) with commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscribing a circle in an equilateral and equiangular pentagon (IV.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: Therefore the circle described with centre F and distance one of the straight lines FG, FH, FK, FL, FM will pass also through the remaining points; and it will touch the straight lines AH, EC, CD, DE, EA, because the angles at the points H, K, M are right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct perpendiculars from the intersection point of the angle-bisectors (or appropriate centre F) to the sides; these perpendiculars are equal so a circle with centre F and radius equal to those perpendicular lengths passes through the tangent points and touches each side (a radius to a tangent makes a right angle). If it did not touch but cut, a contradiction with the property that a right angle at the end of a diameter cannot fall within the circle (cf. III.16) is obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumscribing a circle about an equilateral and equiangular pentagon (IV.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the angles BCD, CDE be bisected by the straight lines CF, DF respectively; and from the point F at which the straight lines meet, let the straight lines FB, FA, FE be joined to the points B, A, E. ... Therefore the circle described with centre F and distance one of the straight lines FA, FB, FC, FD, FE will pass also through the remaining points, and will have been circumscribed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bisect the interior angles of the regular pentagon; the bisectors concur at the center F. Join this center to the vertices: the distances to vertices are equal, so a circle centred at F with that radius passes through all vertices (circumscribes the pentagon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscribing an equilateral and equiangular hexagon in a given circle (IV.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ABCDEF be the given circle; draw the diameter AD; let the centre G be taken, and with centre D and distance DG let the circle EGCH be described; let EG, CG be joined and carried through to the points B, F, and let AB, BC, CD, DE, EF, FA be joined. I say that the hexagon ABCDEF is equilateral and equiangular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By constructing equilateral triangles based on radii (or using the center and equal circumferences), the six arcs and hence the six sides are equal. Porism: the side of the inscribed regular hexagon equals the radius of the circle. Drawing tangents at the division points gives a circumscribed regular hexagon; proofs similar to the pentagon case show inscribed/circumscribed circles exist for such hexagons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscribing a fifteen-angled figure equilateral and equiangular in a given circle (IV.16)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the circle ABCD let there be inscribed a side AC of the equilateral triangle inscribed in it, and a side AB of an equilateral pentagon; therefore, of the equal segments of which there are fifteen in the circle ABCD, there will be five in the circumference ABC which is one-third of the circle, and there will be three in the circumference AB which is one-fifth of the circle; therefore in the remainder BC there will be two of the equal segments. Let BC be bisected at E; therefore each of the circumferences BE, EC is a fifteenth of the circle ABCD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the subdivision given by inscribing a triangle (thirds) and a pentagon (fifths) so that combining those arcs and bisecting the leftover arc yields fifteenths; join the division points to form an equilateral and equiangular 15-gon. Tangents at division points yield a circumscribed 15-gon; similar proofs show inscribed/circumscribed circles exist for that polygon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubling procedure for regular polygons (porism following IV.16)
rubrics_metrics.description: When any regular polygon is given, we can construct a regular polygon with twice the number of sides by first describing a circle about the given polygon and then bisecting all the smaller arcs subtended by the sides. By picking that process any number of times, we see that we can by Euclid's methods construct regular polygons with 3·2^n, 4·2^n, 5·2^n, 15·2^n sides, where n is zero or any positive integer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method: circumscribe a circle about the polygon and bisect arcs repeatedly. Starting from constructible base polygons (3, 4, 5, 15) Euclid's methods generate all polygons whose side-count is base·2^n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 1: Magnitude (Book V)
rubrics_metrics.description: A magnitude is a part of a magnitude, the less of the greater, when it measures the greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology for treating continuous quantities; used as the primitive notion for ratios and proportion in Book V.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 2: Multiple
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater is a multiple of the less when it is measured by the less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard Euclidean notion: 'measured by' means an integral number of times equals the other magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 3: Ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: A ratio is a sort of relation in respect of size between two magnitudes of the same kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduces ratio as a relation of magnitude; note and commentary explain how the term extends to incommensurables by approximation and comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 4: Having a ratio to one another
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnitudes are said to have a ratio to one another which are capable, when multiplied, of exceeding one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excludes infinite magnitudes or infinitesimals; ensures we compare finite magnitudes of the same species that can be made to exceed by taking multiples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 5: Same ratio (Eudoxean definition of proportion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnitudes are said to be in the same ratio, the first to the second and the third to the fourth, when, if any equimultiples whatever be taken of the first and third, and any equimultiples whatever of the second and fourth, the former equimultiples alike exceed, are alike equal to, or alike fall short of, the latter equimultiples respectively taken in corresponding order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central Eudoxean test using equimultiples. Extensive commentary (De Morgan illustration: columns and railings) demonstrates necessity and sufficiency: for every choice of equimultiples the comparative ordering (>, =, <) must match between the first/second pair and the third/fourth pair. This definition handles commensurable and incommensurable magnitudes uniformly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 6: Proportional
rubrics_metrics.description: Let magnitudes which have the same ratio be called proportional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology: 'proportional' = 'in the same ratio' as defined by Def. 5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 7: Greater ratio among pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: When, of the equimultiples, the multiple of the first magnitude exceeds the multiple of the second, but the multiple of the third does not exceed the multiple of the fourth, then the first is said to have a greater ratio to the second than the third has to the fourth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for comparing magnitudes' ratios by comparing corresponding equimultiples; formalizes 'greater' in ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 8: A proportion in three terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A proportion in three terms is the least possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduces short-hand notion: when three magnitudes are in proportion, this is the minimal (simplest) proportional configuration for later definitions (duplicate, triplicate, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 9: Duplicate ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: When three magnitudes are proportional, the first is said to have to the third the duplicate ratio of that which it has to the second.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duplicate = square of the ratio; terminology for powers of ratios when four or more magnitudes are continuously proportional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 10: Triplicate and continued ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: When four magnitudes are continuously proportional, the first is said to have to the fourth the triplicate ratio of that which it has to the second, and so on continually, whatever be the proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology: triplicate = cube of the ratio; extends to any multiplicative repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 11: Corresponding magnitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: The term corresponding magnitudes is used of antecedents in relation to antecedents, and of consequents in relation to consequents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies language when comparing pairs in proportion statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 12: Alternate ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternate ratio means taking the antecedent in relation to the antecedent and the consequent in relation to the consequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operation on a proportion exchanging terms: (A:B :: C:D) → (A:C :: B:D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 13: Inverse ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Inverse ratio means taking the consequent as antecedent in relation to the antecedent as consequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operation on a proportion reversing antecedent and consequent in each pair: (A:B :: C:D) → (B:A :: D:C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 14: Composition of a ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition of a ratio means taking the antecedent together with the consequent as one in relation to the consequent by itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine terms to form new ratio (A+B):B; useful in algebraic manipulations of proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 15: Separation of a ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Separation of a ratio means taking the excess by which the antecedent exceeds the consequent in relation to the consequent by itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separation yields (A−B):B; inverse operation to composition; used in subtraction/analysis of ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 16: Conversion of a ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversion of a ratio means taking the antecedent in relation to the excess by which the antecedent exceeds the consequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form of transforming a ratio to compare antecedent with its excess over consequent; used in Euclidean proportion proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 17: Ratio ex aequali
rubrics_metrics.description: A ratio ex aequali arises when, there being several magnitudes and another set equal to them in multitude which taken two and two are in the same proportion, as the first is to the last among the first magnitudes, so is the first to the last among the second magnitudes; or, in other words, it means taking the extreme terms by virtue of the removal of the intermediate terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the principle of removing intermediates in proportional chains to obtain ratios of extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 18: Perturbed proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: A perturbed proportion arises when, there being three magnitudes and another set equal to them in multitude, as antecedent is to consequent among the first magnitudes, so is antecedent to consequent among the second magnitudes, while, as the consequent is to a third among the first magnitudes, so is a third to the antecedent among the second magnitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the less common 'perturbed' or mixed proportional arrangement used in some Euclidean arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for comparing incommensurables (note on Def. 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: To describe the relative magnitude of two incommensurables of the same kind one can provide arbitrarily close rational approximations (e.g., the diagonal S and side D of a square: show D lies between 1.414213 and 1.414214 times S), and carry approximations to any desired degree of accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The explanatory note argues that although incommensurables cannot be expressed as exact rational multiples, their ratio can be determined to any precision by successive approximations (decimal or sexagesimal), and Euclid's theory of proportion is capable of handling such comparisons via the Eudoxean definition and approximation methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative model and justification of Def. 5 (De Morgan's columns-and-railings)
rubrics_metrics.description: De Morgan's illustration: two colonnades/rows with spacings C and R — the distribution/order of 'railings' among 'columns' determines the ratio; if, for every choice of equimultiples, the comparative order (> = <) of multiples matches between pairs, then the ratios are the same. Any small change in one distance eventually changes distribution, proving necessity and sufficiency of Euclid's test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This model is presented as an intuitive justification that Euclid's equimultiple test (Def. 5) is both necessary and sufficient to capture the ordinary notion of 'same ratio', and it addresses criticisms that the definition is 'infinite' by showing practical tests via large but finite multiples and the stability/instability of orders under perturbation.
